new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Copies checked (55 pp.) and its extracted text, plus chapter 1, bibliography and in the same directory. Locator verified: extracted text of PDF p. 48 of the chapter-3 bitstream carries printed page number 92 and contains sec. 3.1.5.4 'Reduced Syllable' and 3.1.5.5 'Sesquisyllable' exactly as quoted, including the original typos ('ralatively', 'follwing', 'syllble'): 'In case of some Darlong disyllabic words, the length of nucleus in initial open syllables contrastively become short and get centralised to an extent and, because of this phenomenon the preceding syllable become phonetically reduces stress and ralatively less prominent than the follwing syllable.' followed by '..'sesquisyllabic…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Darlong is described as a two-tone (H/L register) language; no word-stress rule is given as such. The only prominence statement is iambic: in disyllables (notably prefix/proclitic + root, e.g. /a-vɔk/ -> [ɐ.vɔk] 'his pig', /ki-pa:/ -> [kɪ.pa:] 'my father', /in-kʰai/ -> [ɪn.kʰai] 'to move') the initial open syllable is shortened and centralised, carries reduced stress and is less prominent than the following (root/final) syllable, i.e. a weak+strong sesquisyllabic pattern with prominence on the second/full syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: The reduction is stated for 'some Darlong disyllabic words'; the examples are possessive/agreement proclitics a-, ki- and the verbal prefix in-/i- before roots. Nothing is said about prominence in trisyllables (said to be the commonest word shape) or in compounds beyond tone sandhi (H+H -> H L).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (prefix/proclitic + root phonological words, citation forms elicited in fieldwork, Praat pitch tracks for tone pairs). The thesis frames suprasegmental phonology as tone + vowel length only; the stress remark sits in the syllable-typology section, so this is a tonal description with an incidental iambic-prominence observation, not a worked-out stress analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Brahma 2018 describes Darlong as spoken in Tripura (Kumarghat/Kailashahar area, Unakoti and North Tripura districts), classed by the author within Central Kuki-Chin close to Mizo/Hmar; this is the darl1242 / ISO dln variety itself, not a differently named dialect.

new_statements.quote: There are a good number or words in the Darlong language which have more than one meanings. The meanings are ascertained through the tones, accents and through the relevancy of the context. There are three main tones - the upward, the downward and the level. the vowels (except 0) have two main sounds indicated by placing a circumflex accent on the long one to distinguish it from the short one. Hence the words having more than one meanings are not as confusing as one might think, as the tone, sounds and accents are taken into account.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing statement from Brahma 2018 (tone language with a prominence remark): both agree Darlong is tonal; Darlong 1995 reports three tones (upward, downward, level) where Brahma 2018 describes two register tones (H/L) plus tone sandhi, a tone-inventory difference, not a stress difference. Darlong 1995 adds nothing on stress placement, so it neither confirms nor contradicts Brahma's iambic-like 'reduced initial syllable, following syllable more prominent' observation. The catalog record itself has an empty rule; this work supports only the 'tonal' part.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The book says Darlong has three tones (rising, falling, level) that distinguish homographs, and uses 'accent' only for the circumflex that marks long vowels in the orthography (p. 61: 'A circumflex is put on A, Aw, E, I and U to give long sounds'). It says nothing about where word stress falls or whether stress exists. The only other use of 'accent' (p. ~54, 'The main difference between these sub-tribes [Awmhroi and Fatlei] lies in the accent of the dialects') means dialectal pronunciation, not word stress. The pronunciation guide (p. 60) adds only that 'a' is 'often rather longer when at the end of the syllable'.
new_statements.identity_note: Darlong 1995 (p. ~54) notes two sub-tribes, Awmhroi and Fatlei, whose dialects once differed 'in the accent', a difference the author says has been 'almost totally done away with through intermixing'; the language chapter describes the merged standard Darlong (Hriam) of Tripura, written in the Mizo-derived Roman orthography. It also mentions a former intermediate dialect 'Chungtlang tawng' (between Lushei and Darlong) now known only to a few elderly speakers.

sources.note: Ch. 3 'Phonology' (pp. 45-99) treats suprasegmentals as tone (two register tones H/L with tone sandhi, sec. 3.2.1-3.2.3) and vowel length (3.2.4); there is no stress section and the word 'stress' occurs once: sec. 3.1.5.4-3.1.5.5 (p. 92) says the initial open syllable of some disyllables is shortened/centralised and 'reduces stress and relatively less prominent than the following syllable', and that Darlong words pattern as sesquisyllabic 'weak syllable followed by a strong syllable' (iambic). Ch. 2 states 'There are no available linguistic researches on Darlong language.'
